content: Nitroglycerin skin patches are prescribed to prevent chest pain, also known as angina. These patches function by relaxing the blood vessels that supply the heart, thereby improving blood flow and oxygen delivery to the heart. In some cases, this medication may be prescribed for other purposes. If you have questions about its use, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Nitroglycerin skin patches are applied directly to the skin, typically once a day. Your doctor may instruct you to remove the patch at a specific time each day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use the patch exactly as directed. Do not apply it more or less frequently than prescribed. While nitroglycerin patches help control chest pain, they do not cure it. Continue using the patches even if you feel well, and do not stop using them without consulting your doctor, as abrupt discontinuation may lead to chest pain. Apply the patch to clean, dry skin that is relatively free of hair, such as the area above your knee or upper arm above the elbow. Avoid applying the patch to irritated, scarred, broken, or calloused skin. Rotate the application site daily to prevent skin irritation. Always remove the old patch before applying a new one. If the patch becomes loose or falls off, replace it with a fresh one. After use, fold the patch in half with the sticky sides together and dispose of it carefully, as it still contains active medication that could be harmful to children or pets. Nitroglycerin may lose its effectiveness over time due to tolerance. If your angina attacks become more frequent, last longer, or are more severe, contact your doctor immediately. Before using a nitroglycerin skin patch, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to nitroglycerin in any form (patches, tablets, capsules, or ointments), isosorbide (e.g., Imdur, Isordil, Sorbitrate), or any other medications. Also, disclose if you have or have ever had anemia, glaucoma, or recent head trauma. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while using the patch, notify your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures, inform the healthcare provider that you are using a nitroglycerin patch. This medication may cause drowsiness or dizziness. Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you. Ask your doctor about the safe use of alcohol while using this medication, as alcohol can exacerbate its side effects. If you forget to apply a patch, do so as soon as you remember. Do not apply two patches to make up for a missed dose. Common side effects of nitroglycerin patches include headache, skin irritation or rash, dizziness, upset stomach, and flushing (a sensation of warmth). If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects, such as blurred vision, dry mouth, chest pain, or fainting, require immediate medical attention. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor can report it to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store this medication at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture, and out of reach of children. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Nitroglycerin skin patches are not intended for acute angina attacks. Continue using nitroglycerin tablets or spray for chest pain that has already started. If headaches persist, consult your doctor about taking acetaminophen. Do not take aspirin or other headache medications while using nitroglycerin patches unless directed by your doctor. Do not share your medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist.
